Law firm apologizes to truckers for ‘serial killer’ ad

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.
  • In a recent development, the full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves.
  • The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

In a recent development, the full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”.

Industry observers note that in its statement, the law firm states it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”.

Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under new ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Senate confirmed Justice Joseph Story to the Supreme Court on this day in 1811. When he joined three months later at age 32, he became the youngest justice in Supreme Court history, as we noted in a Closer Look in May.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, Dec. 4. The disputes address such challenges as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys. For more on the conference, see the On Site section below.

The December argument session will begin on Monday, Nov. 30.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

The judge noted certain emails sent by Secretary Brooke Rollins amounted to coercion and violated employees' constitutional rights.

According to recent reports, SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â Shortly after assuming her position as U.S. secretary of agriculture, Brooke Rollins began sending a series of holiday emails to all USDA employees invoking Christianity. Employees sued, claiming the messages pressured them to conform to the secretaryâs religious beliefs and made them feel unwelcome.

On Thursday, a federal judge ordered Rollins to cease the messages, quoting the secretary’s own guidance on religious expression in the workplace in her 21-page ruling granting the employeesâ request for a preliminary injunction.

It has been revealed that âThe court orders that the secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages. She â[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [her] to stop,â she â[c]annot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances,â and she â[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates,ââ U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson wrote.

The Joe Biden appointee continued: âShe may â[d]iscuss [her] religious beliefs with interested colleagues,â â[s]hare why [her] faith is meaningful to [her],â â[p]olitely invite coworkers to religious services or events,â â[e]xpress religious viewpoints during appropriate conversations.ââ.

The judge additionally clarified that her injunction blocks Rollinsâ use of her official email âin a manner that also prevents non-parties from receiving constitutionally violative messages,â because the government does not allow employees to opt out of the secretaryâs messages.

The seven named plaintiffs, described as âa group of multifaith and nonreligious USDA employees,â claim Rollins had been violating the First Amendment by sending a series of âincreasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce.â.

In a recent development, in one email, sent on Dec. 23, 2025, Rollins states in a video that âthe spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life.â.

In another message, sent on April 5, 2026, Rollins extolled âthe greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankindâ and described her employees as âlike the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord â¦ almost 2,000 years ago.â.

In their complaint, the plaintiffs describe the emails as âexactly the sort of government-sponsored religious coercion, religious sermonizing, and denominational preference that the establishment clause prohibits.â.

Thompson agreed, ruling the December 2025 and April 2026 emails âgo too farâ and âsuggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an establishment clause violation.â.

The judge routinely referenced Rollinsâ November 2025 guidance throughout her ruling, writing the court âfinds the secretaryâs guidance reasoned.â However, Thompson emphasized Rollins needs to âobserve her own directives.â.

âWhy should the secretary be exempt from her own rules? The buck stops with Secretary Rollins. In fact, her position of authority warrants greater concern as she sits atop the agency hierarchy,â she wrote.

The judge called Rollinsâ use of her official email account to send department-wide religious emails worrisome, agreeing with the plaintiffs that the secretary’s emails are mandatory to read, as she also uses her official email for other key messages, such as agency reorganization and intends for a government shutdown.

âUSDA employees are expected to read the secretaryâs religious message. To suggest that plaintiffs may choose at their discretion which of the secretaryâs emails to read and which to ignore defies logic,â she wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the judge repeatedly stated the court had no view on what Rollins could or couldnât do in her personal capacity, noting that the secretary is not shy about her religious beliefs. However, Thompson said Rollins’ actions were âthe type of conduct the Framers sought to protect against.â.

âThe Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that âimmense social pressureâ can result in a finding of coercion. Such pressure is demonstrated here,â she added.

While the judge sided with the plaintiffs on their constitutional claims, she tossed their claim that the emails violated the Administrative Procedure Act, finding they were not a final agency action or an order.

DOJ representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

    LOS ANGELES (CN) â Federal prosecutors charged 14 people with stealing more than $22 million worth of Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, JBL electronics and Crocs from freight trains in Southern California over the past two years.

    In a recent development, the crew was led by a 21-year-old man from East Los Angeles and included his father and two of his uncles, according to an announcement Thursday by the U.S. attorney’s office in LA.

    Industry observers note that âThe scale of the theft is staggering," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli mentioned in the statement. âWe will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash.â.

    The crew targeted freight trains that haul the millions of containers with overseas imports that arrive every year at the ports of LA and Long Beach to destinations in the Central U.S.

    Once they had selected a “high-value” train to rob, prosecutors say in the indictment, a group of burglars would board the train at the tracks. At a predetermined point along the tracks, the burglars cut the air hoses that control the train’s brakes, bringing it to an emergency halt.

    Other crew members would be ready with trucks and vans to promptly collect the boxes of shoes and other merchandise from the train and take them to their stash houses.

    Some crew members would contact buyers, including one unidentified retailer who repeatedly bought large quantities of Nike sneakers from the train robbers.

    Industry observers note that “On July 14, 2025, at approximately 12:13 p.m., defendant Marquina offered to sell defendant a Firm 1 representative 600 pairs of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers for $60 each, claiming they retailed for $125 each,” the prosecutors wrote. “The Company 1 representative responded, ‘Iâll buy all air forces … Bring asap.’”.

    The next day, this defendant asked the firm to pay him in cash because the banks were âtripping.â.

    The crew wasn’t shy about flaunting their riches in selfies with stacks of stolen merchandise and cash, as well as making videos of themselves while burglarizing the trains.

    They also created a group chat on Instagram called “Los Trenes,” where they discussed their thefts as they were happening.

    “On July 15, 2026, at approximately 1:57 a.m., defendant Rodolfo Angel posted to the Los Trenes Group Chat, ‘Train still over there?’ At approximately 2:23 a.m., defendant Estrada posted, ‘Stopped it good,’ and defendant Sanchez replied, ‘Whoop,’” prosecutors stated in the indictment.

    The trains were stopped and robbed along tracks in industrial areas southeast of downtown LA and elsewhere in Southern California.

    The defendants are charged with conspiracy, theft of interstate railroad cargo, possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo and violence against railroad carriers.

    The court docket didn’t yet list lawyers representing the defendants.

    A Ninth Circuit panel questioned whether DHS regulations prohibiting loud or unusual noise near federal buildings give officers too much discretion to restrict protests.

    Recent findings suggest that (CN) âÂ On the inside of a federal building in Eugene, Oregon, IRS workers interviewed taxpayers. On the outside, protesters blared megaphones in opposition to the Trump administrationâs immigration policies.

    It has been revealed that the government called it a disruption. The protesters called it free speech.

    According to recent reports, A federal judge in Oregon blocked the Trump administration earlier this year from enforcing newly introduced regulations that prohibited protesters from making unusual noise at federal buildings that could disrupt workers. But the government was back in court Thursday to ask a Ninth Circuit panel to reverse that order.

    Industry observers note that âThe regulatory provision at glitch in this case reflects the common sense notion that loud or unusual noise emanating from right outside a federal building can disrupt government operations, just as loud or unusual noise inside the building can,â Department of Justice attorney Brian Springer told a three-judge panel. âThese sorts of noise restrictions are long-standing and prevalent throughout the law.â.

    The lower court had found the new regulation on noise was too vague under the Fifth Amendmentâs due process clause, but Springer countered that, saying “the Supreme Court, this court and federal courts of appeals across the country have repeatedly and consistently upheld similar provisions against vagueness challenges like the one here, because the language affords fair notice about what conduct is covered.”.

    However, Springer met resistance from all three members of the panel, all Joe Biden appointees, who questioned the governmentâs citation of related cases in its opening brief, as well as its use of language in the regulations prohibiting unusual noise.

    âI think anyone would appreciate that the megaphone use at glitch here was precisely the type of activity that would be likely to affect people working inside this office building,â Springer told the panel.

    But the judges also questioned how much discretion federal officers would have to enforce the regulations and whether the regulations could apply in different types of federal buildings.

    âWhat if it’s next to a busy street?" U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung asked. “There’s a traffic jam, someone starts honking, people inside the federal building can hear it, they seem to be affected by a loud or unusual noise. Would that subject them? Would that be a violation?â.

    Springer noted the noise has to actually affect the operations of the building.

    In a recent development, âThat’s exactly the question, and you’re not answering it, so I’m really interested in whether the answer is yes or no,â U.S. Circuit Judge Roopali Desai stated. âIf it could affect the operations of an individual inside the federal building, would it be a violation of this regulation? And if the answer is no, why not?â.

    It depends, Springer said, adding âI think a fleeting honk is very unlikely to violate the regulation.â.

    âIt’s loud or unusual noise in areas outside of property that affects persons on the federal property,â Sung continued. âSo if I can hear it, and it’s loud, why isn’t that affecting me?â.

    âYour honor, the sorts of affects that the agency is looking for are the ones that we have in this case, where plaintiffs were using ââ.

    âBut you need something in the regulation that narrows it to those ‘affects,’â Sung interrupted. âWhat is the plain meaning of âaffectâ? Because normally, I think, in plain meaning, affect has a very broad meaning.â.

    Marianne Dugan, representing the protesters who sued after the regulations were issued, argued that the exchange with the government attorney illustrated why the regulation was facially unconstitutional and could not be narrowed.

    Recent findings suggest that âYou have this word âaffects,â which gives almost total discretion to anybody reading it who’s enforcing that rule to say, âYour noise is affecting the people in this building,ââ mentioned Dugan, an attorney with the Eugene-based Civil Liberties Defense Center. âThe district court’s factual findings are not clearly erroneous, its conclusions of law were legally correct and the scope of the injunction is not an abuse of discretion.".

    The regulation has a chilling effect on ordinary people who want to protest at federal buildings, she said. Despite the preliminary injunction, a protester was threatened as recently as Wednesday with a citation, she added.

    The protesters filed their lawsuit in December 2025, after they were cited and arrested for violating the regulations that went into affect the previous month. They are seeking a permanent injunction of the regulation.

    The protesters have established regular protests outside of the Eugene federal building, which is next to the office for Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Circuit Judge Ana de Alba joined Sung and Desai on the panel.

    #8449. An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1333 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • According to recent reports, iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • Recent findings suggest that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is right now considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    According to recent reports, iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    Recent findings suggest that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    Industry observers note that in two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    It has been revealed that in addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    In a recent development, the solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    In a recent development, but the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    In a recent development, once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

    âHow can the system survive if the general public thinks that judges have skin in the game?â asked one judge on the Upcoming York Court of Appeals.

    (CN) â In 2023, defendant Glaston Gaines was given a choice: face up to 25 years in prison for a robbery charge or plead guilty and waive his right to appeal in exchange for a sentencing commitment of 10 to 13 years from the trial judge.

    It has been revealed that he chose the latter, and was ultimately sentenced to 12 years in prison for his role in the crime. But the maneuver from the judge was under the microscope of the Latest York Court of Appeals on Thursday, as the seven-judge panel grappled with whether court-initiated appeal waivers should be lawful at all.

    Gaines claims they arenât. His lawyer, Legal Aid attorney Sarod Nori, told the stateâs high court that these waivers are âa threat to the legitimacy of the criminal justice system,â since it amounts to coercion from the trial judge â who is supposed to be impartial.

    Recent findings suggest that in Gainesâ case, the appeal waiver wasnât part of his plea deal with the prosecution at all. Instead, it was tacked on as an added requirement from the court in exchange for the commitment to the sentencing time range.

    âA sentence is not a bargaining chip that a judge can use,â Nori argued.

    What ensued was a debate over the intended purpose of a court-initiated appeal waiver in the first place. Nori suggested they are an option for judges âin the interest of finality,â so criminal cases can be closed without victims having to reopen old wounds in the appellate process. Judge Madeline Singas brought up a hypothetical of a 9-year-old rape victim, whom a judge might want to protect from the proceedings by offering such a waiver agreement for sentencing.

    Chief Judge Rowan Wilson took it a different way.

    Sources indicate that âThe reason we have appeal waivers is so the system doesnât get flooded with cases we canât try because there’s too many of them,â he stated. âItâs really an efficiency point, no?â.

    Either way, Nori maintained itâs an unlawful tool in the trial courtâs belt. According to court filings, Gaines told his judge, âI feel like I have no choiceâ but to accept the appeal waiver when he pleaded guilty. He was also denied the opportunity to speak at his plea hearing after the judge told him to save it for sentencing.

    Even the state admitted that may have been a misstep.

    âI will concede that if the defendant is asking to say something, that the judge should probably allow him to say it,â state attorney April Orlowski told the court Thursday.

    In a recent development, judge Michael Garcia suggested these challenges could just be handled on a case-by-case basis by the appellate division. While an appeal waiver generally prevents a defendant from appealing most aspects of their conviction and sentence, they can still make a challenge if the deal itself was made in bad faith â as Gaines claims his was.

    In a recent development, the court didnât immediately issue a ruling following the hearing. But several of its judges offered up critiques about the optics of greenlighting the practice. Judge Caitlin Halligan said it could lead to an appearance of bias for a judge since it âinsulatesâ their decision from further review.

    Judge Jenny Rivera expressed similar concerns.

    âHow can the system survive if the general public thinks that judges have skin in the game, that theyâre interested in a particular outcome, that theyâre seeking favoritism for one side over the other?â she asked.

    Industry observers note that laws surrounding court-initiated appeal waivers vary from state to state. Newly introduced York has taken a nuanced approach to the matter, defined largely by a 1989 ruling in *People v. Seaberg,*which found that a defendant can indeed waive their appellate rights in exchange for a more favorable sentence from the court. But earlier this year in People v. Turner, a mid-level state appellate court found that the trial court must provide an on-the-record rationale for their appeal waiver.

    #8445. Latest Update: The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1583 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent latest book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent latest book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    Recent findings suggest that shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    Recent findings suggest that but this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    Chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    In a recent development, marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    Industry observers note that justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    Recent findings suggest that and in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The New York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    It has been revealed that shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Newly introduced York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to glitch a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    Sources indicate that in the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a fresh story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    If I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    Recent findings suggest that regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    Attorneys make closing arguments in Libby Mine reinsurance case

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Omaha-based National Indemnity sued after reinsurance company TIG did not cover its losses.
    • According to recent reports, OMAHA, Neb.
    • Nearly two weeks of arguments in the Libby Mine reinsurance case came to a close Thursday at the federal courthouse in downtown Omaha, with the case going to the eight-person jury late in the Nebraska afternoon as the sky outside darkened and commuters hurried home.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Omaha-based National Indemnity sued after reinsurance company TIG did not cover its losses. National Indemnity insured the state of Montana, which was found to have failed to warn about the asbestos danger in and around the small city of Libby.

    According to recent reports, OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â A local jury’s decision in a reinsurance case connected to the mass asbestos exposure at Libby Mine in northwest Montana may come down to whether it believes a company under the umbrella of hometown business hero Warren Buffett lied to its reinsurer.

    Nearly two weeks of arguments in the Libby Mine reinsurance case came to a close Thursday at the federal courthouse in downtown Omaha, with the case going to the eight-person jury late in the Nebraska afternoon as the sky outside darkened and commuters hurried home. Jurors did not render a verdict, and deliberation will begin Friday morning.

    Omaha-based National Indemnity Insurance Company is suing TIG Insurance Company, one of its reinsurers, after, it indicates, TIG did not pay its claim after National Indemnity and Montana agreed in 2022 to resolve all coverage claims over widespread asbestos contamination from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million. National Indemnity insured Montana for two years in the 1970s.

    TIG claims National Indemnity did not provide adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

    âIt lied," said Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments. “It hid. It moved around numbers. It abused this process to the detriment of its reinsurers.â.

    In his closing argument, Michael Knoerzer, a New York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, stated TIG never took advantage of its opportunities to associate with National Indemnity on the case, but criticized how National Indemnity handled it.

    According to recent reports, âTIG sometimes stated we could have done it better. They are second-guessing. They could have helped; they didnât," he said. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â.

    In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in northwestern Montana.

    From 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about seven miles outside of Libby.

    Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, itself was not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

    Decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

    It has been revealed that thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

    Sources indicate that the fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

    It has been revealed that national Indemnity insured the state of Montana from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975. During that same period, TIG provided it reinsurance coverage.

    According to recent reports, reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance tech giant indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG Insurance Company did not fully do.

    In 2022, National Indemnity and Montana agreed to resolve all coverage claims over widespread asbestos contamination from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

    It has been revealed that national Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers have been dropped from the suit, but TIG remains. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believes it owes â $12.7 million.

    Industry observers note that according to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss. At first, the state said 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

    But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

    Ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, that number came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

    Under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

    At issue in the case is whether individual deaths could count as an occurrence. National Indemnity has argued that it could have found itself on the hook for “billions” if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

    TIG, in its critique of the settlement, indicates Montana consistently argued 21 occurrences for years. Davis went so far as to say the settlement wasn’t a settlement.

    Sources indicate that “You have to have a signed document to have a settlement. You have to have an agreement to have a settlement. They didnât have any of that,” Davis told the jury. “An unconditional payment is not a settlement.”.

    National Indemnity is owned by Berkshire Hathaway, whose chairman until recently was Buffett. On the first day of trial, National Indemnity President Donald Wurster testified he felt the need to tell Buffett when the Montana Supreme Court found the state responsible for not warning the miners, and that the state requested that National Indemnity take over defense of the claim.

    VANCOUVER, British Columbia (CN) â Steelworkers protesting a copper mine can’t continue picketing outside a British Columbia port terminal, a judge ruled Thursday.

    In a recent development, granting an injunction to the port’s operator, PKM Canada Services Inc., B.C. Supreme Court Justice Simon Coval mentioned United Steelworkers Local 7619 and its allied organizations’ actions outside the port were likely illegal under the province’s Labour Relations Code.

    B.C.âs Labour Relations Code restricts picketing at locations outside a unionâs direct workplace, and USW had expanded its strike against Teck Resourcesâ Highland Valley Copper mine to PKM’s port terminal in North Vancouver.

    It has been revealed that coval sided with PKM and the B.C. Marine Employersâ Association, which sued sued last Tuesday and argued in court Monday that the port activities constituted an illegal secondary picket.

    Ruling from the bench, the judge broadly agreed with PKM’s claim the picket had caused irreversible damage, and that without an injunction, the port was at further risk.

    Attorney Ryan Copeland, representing PKM, argued that refusal by longshore workers to cross the picket line led to significant business disruptions over multiple days.

    According to recent reports, labor advocacy organization B.C. Federation of Labour, which ordered a âhot edictâ against other unionized workers handling the mineâs materials, and a variety of other local unions also joined the picket outside the port.

    Copeland said the longshore workers ignored Canada Industrial Relations Board orders to cross the picket line and that the picket even continued into the morning of Nov. 9, despite an order by the B.C. Labour Relations Board barring the picket line the night before.

    In a recent development, coval rejected arguments by the USW and the federation that the orders from the B.C. Labour Relations Board and Canada Industrial Relations Board were enough.

    The judge also noted the federal labor board canât order the steelworkers not to picket the location â though it can order the longshore workers to cross the picket line â and that PKM doesnât have standing to maintain or enforce the provincial labor board orders against picketing.

    âThe BCLRB order may be amended or terminated at any time,â Coval said, echoing Copelandâs arguments that PKM is at the mercy of Teckâs decisions around enforcing or maintaining the order.

    Sources indicate that teck Resources itself has sued over the picketing at both its mine and PKM’s port. A court ruled last week to halt some activities but not picketing altogether at the mine.

    Coval said the more challenging question to answer was whether the injunction was still necessary.

    Sources indicate that though the picket line initially continued after the B.C. Labour Relations Board order, the union lawyers mentioned the fact that there hadnât been any picketing or related activity at the port terminal for a week as of the Monday hearing suggested there was no need for an injunction.

    They stated they were also willing to agree not to return to the terminal without reasonable notice to PKM.

    âWe donât anticipate coming back,â said the federationâs lawyer, Chris Buchanan, on Monday. USWâs lawyer, William Clements, said the same.

    But Coval was unconvinced by that, pointing to the continued picket after the initial labor boardsâ orders.

    âThe defendantsâ insistence on retaining the ability to revive the picket line with reasonable notice reflects their position that they have the right to carry out the impugned conduct,â Coval mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that PKM and the B.C. Marine Employersâ Association are still seeking damages from USW and the B.C. Federation of Labour for the economic impact of that picket line.

    Arguments for that will be heard in trial at a future, yet-to-be-determined date.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • Before we explore some of the major complications pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    Before we explore some of the major complications pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    Litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the problem is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    After a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    Once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court introduces in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    In a recent development, the court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    Recent findings suggest that for a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely announces that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    Once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile problems that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    Industry observers note that one week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    This ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    In a recent development, shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either currently serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    It has been revealed that in March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    On Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    As expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    This week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    Industry observers note that nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    Last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the concern will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    In addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    In a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    According to recent reports, because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    Sources indicate that as I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration complications dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    Industry observers note that and there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    Suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    According to recent reports, the responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    Recent findings suggest that the rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    Sources indicate that several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are currently considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, Newly introduced Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the company. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    Sources indicate that the responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    It has been revealed that in its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to matter universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    According to recent reports, after CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    The case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    In a recent development, that deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    Industry observers note that the justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #8435. Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1322 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • According to recent reports, as Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify.
    • Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    According to recent reports, as Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton noted the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

    Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

    It is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

    So how can one tell the difference?

    As we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

    According to recent reports, political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

    In a recent development, the 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each new circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

    But circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

    Timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

    To clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This shows, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

    Finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

    In a recent development, the allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”.

    It has been revealed that jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.
