    Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that originally published on Nov.
    • The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon.
    • Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

    The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”.

    Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he confirmed that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

    After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

    In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

    When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

    It has been revealed that on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it problems a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Philips Sonicare Polishes Its Streaming TV Strategy Using Amazon Ads Agent

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brushing your teeth is a chore, and so is trying to buy streaming TV ad inventory publisher by publisher.
    • During the 2025-26 upfront season, Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself.
    • In both cases, the rationale for consolidation is simplification.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brushing your teeth is a chore, and so is trying to buy streaming TV ad inventory publisher by publisher.

    During the 2025-26 upfront season, Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself. Amazon recently centralized its Amazon DSP has been replaced by a upcoming product called DVA+ (which stands for “display, video and audio”).

    In both cases, the rationale for consolidation is simplification. When media workflows merge, ad transactions need fewer dashboards and third parties, which improves campaign efficiency and performance.

    Philips Sonicare, which was already using Amazon’s Sponsored Ads to market its products on the flagship site, but wanted to expand its target audience after finding that 86% of the oral care audience segment was not considering Philips products.

    To reach them, the brand paired Amazon’s data with its own first-party data to create custom audience segments of customers who are in market for oral care products but haven’t shopped from Philips before.

    As part of its upfront commitment, Philips used Amazon Ads Agent to buy streaming media across Paramount+, Roku, Tubi, Peacock, TelevisaUnivision and Warner Bros. Discovery. Previously, it had to work with each of these publishers separately.

    By consolidating its buys, Philips saw 24% incremental reach it saw among audiences likely to be interested in its products, as well as a 75% reduction in customer cost per acquisition.

    For brands, centralizing multi-platform streaming buys improves visibility across channels, which helps advertisers learn more about their audience and adjust their campaigns accordingly.

    “By working with Amazon Ads to consolidate our streaming TV investment, we can apply one audience strategy across our portfolio, and manage reach and frequency more effectively while better understanding what happens after an ad is seen,” Priyanti Telang, director of Amazon activation, retail media and digital shelf excellence for Philips North America, told me.

    Using one buying platform also helps Philips speed up reporting.

    Buying media and pulling reports from several platforms is “highly inefficient” because there is audience overlap, remarked Chris Conetta, director of omnichannel supply for Amazon Ads, so marketers “lose a lot of the incrementality you get when using one tool that can measure audiences across multiple touchpoints.”.

    Sources indicate that that logic applies beyond just Amazon’s platform. Amazon (and other retailers, for that matter) can also attract brands seeking more purchase data to improve their performance and attribution, including on streaming TV.

    Since TV is in its performance era, it’s not surprising that Philips was keen to prove streaming’s impact.

    One of the clearest findings from its media consolidation effort, Telang noted, is that “streaming can generate measurable intent.” After seeing the brand’s connected TV ads, more consumers searched online for Philips products by name, she said, and “that intent translated into purchases.”.

    Philips saw a 15x higher purchase rate among consumers who saw the ads on streaming TV than among consumers who only saw a Sponsored Ads placement for Philips online.

    Conetta noted, however, that this increase was a result of customers seeing Philips ads across both streaming and on Amazon’s site. An Amazon executive would say that, but Conetta has a point. Industry research suggests that diversified ad formats can drive improved brand results.

    Philips Sonicare’s experience also notes something about streaming TV’s place in the marketing funnel, Telang said, “as a contributor to commercial performance as well as brand awareness.” Guess reach and performance complement each other like brushing and flossing.

    In other words, brace yourselves (ha) to hear more about “full-funnel” advertising in CTV advertising discussions.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The best AI use cases in ad sales aren’t flashy.
    • That’s been the case at The Wall Street Journal, where AI is quietly taking over most of the busywork for the ad sales team, claims Josh Stinchcomb, the Journal’s global CRO, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.
    • For example, what seller doesn’t know the frustration of trying to track down a stat buried somewhere in an old email thread or Slack channel when they’re trying to get ready for a meeting?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The best AI use cases in ad sales aren’t flashy. Mostly, it’s about automating the tasks nobody wanted to do anyway.

    That’s been the case at The Wall Street Journal, where AI is quietly taking over most of the busywork for the ad sales team, claims Josh Stinchcomb, the Journal’s global CRO, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.

    For example, what seller doesn’t know the frustration of trying to track down a stat buried somewhere in an old email thread or Slack channel when they’re trying to get ready for a meeting?

    But now, the Journal’s sales team has access to an internal AI-powered search tool that does the digging for them. It can even recap whatever the seller last discussed with a particular prospect so they can walk into their meeting prepared and knowing exactly where the conversation left off.

    According to recent reports, “It’s really helpful for pulling from the information we have available to ourselves but isn’t always at our fingertips,” Stinchcomb says. “That’s been a great time-saver.”.

    There’s also a tool for digital ops that checks line items against ad creative and IOs and also handles taking campaign screenshots, which Stinchcomb describes as a decidedly “laborious and really unfun” task. The result, he claims, is fewer botched campaign launches and less inventory lost to make-goods.

    But the bigger bet is media planning.

    Right now, it takes a planner four or five hours to turn an RFP into a plan, Stinchcomb notes, in part because they have to check inventory across multiple different systems. The Journal is testing a tool, however, that can read RFPs, look at past campaigns for similar audiences and build a recommended plan in about an hour.

    With the team producing thousands of plans a year, that’s a lot of hours back in their lives. The time and effort saved is being redeployed toward larger million-dollar-plus RFPs, where Stinchcomb states the Journal’s win rate has gone up five percentage points. A wider rollout of the tool is planned for early next year.

    In a recent development, “Bringing it all together is a great strategy,” he indicates. “It’s an efficient way to bring in chunks of revenue.”.

    In a recent development, but there’s one place where AI isn’t welcome, though, and that’s in the writing of branded content, which is a growing business for the Journal. WSJ Intelligence, its custom content studio, takes its cue from the Journal’s newsroom. The work might be “facilitated by these tools,” Stinchcomb states, “but not written by them.”.

    “AI is great at sort of rehashing what’s out there,” Stinchcomb says. “It’s not necessarily great at breaking news, as it were, or bringing a fresher perspective.”.

    Branded content has to be as interesting and engaging as anything else that’s out there competing for a reader’s attention.

    And if it commits the sin of being boring or derivative, Stinchcomb notes, then “[people] don’t read it, and I’m not getting paid.”.

    Also in this episode: Why less than 5% of the Journal’s digital ad revenue is programmatic, how WSJ Intelligence keeps its custom research credible, News Corp’s “woo and sue” approach to AI licensing deals and Stinchcomb’s past life as the singer in a “tragic emo-style” band in high school.

    #8422. Breaking: Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (875 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.
    • The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.
    • According to recent reports, zillow knows that challenge well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

    The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

    According to recent reports, zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

    “We are known for dreaming,” noted Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

    That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

    In a recent development, in September, Canvas confirmed a new division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

    The “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?).

    Quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ new division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas states its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

    For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, mentioned Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

    But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, said Lee.

    Recent findings suggest that the agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

    Canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, mentioned Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

    Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting firm Dstillery.

    Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, stated Kandikonda.

    Industry observers note that for instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he noted. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

    According to recent reports, dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

    Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda remarked, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

    The goal behind the upcoming product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

    Increasing ROI is notable for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda remarked, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”.

    So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda said.

    That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

    An off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he remarked, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

    The destination, not the journey.

    From Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

    Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

    According to recent reports, from there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

    The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, said Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”.

    Only You Can Prevent JavaScript Security Hacks; AppLovin Eyes A Criteo Acquisition

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.
    • The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites.
    • “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.

    The list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites. The concern is that many operators don’t audit the tech vendors that drop JavaScript onto their pages.

    “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.

    The “content security policies” (or CSPs) Edwards refers to set limits on what third-party code can do on a site, including what it can load or inject. Of the 178 affected Optimizely accounts, only 24 had CSPs in place and enforced them. Those 24 didn’t spread the malware.

    Because the malware ran in the site’s JavaScript, visitors to pages without CSPs could be infected simply by loading the page – no click or scroll required.

    According to recent reports, the main offender, btw, in terms of third-party JavaScript abusers that expose sites to hackers, is ad tech, of course. It’s not even close. Which is why, unfortunately, as Krebs notes, downloading a modern ad blocker is the best solution for consumers to protect themselves.

    The rumor mill is heating up as the year winds down.

    Recent findings suggest that criteo has been part of that chatter for a while, with private equity firms Vista Equity and Quinti Capital reportedly interested in taking it private. Criteo hasn’t exactly thrived as a public tech giant, after all.

    But it does possess an immense graph of shopper info.

    And now another contender has reportedly entered the ring. According to Reuters, AppLovin is among those in talks with Criteo.

    Big companies can use deal talks to get an inside look at the finances and operations of smaller companies. Even if the deal doesn’t happen, they’ve still gotten a peek under the hood.

    Recent findings suggest that amazon, for example, was rumored to have considered Criteo once upon a time – not long before launching its own off-site retargeting. Hmm.

    But Criteo would be an interesting fit for AppLovin. It plugs into a wide network of retailers and web publishers – an entirely upcoming arena to AppLovin, which operates almost entirely in-app – and would bring a large book of business with ecommerce companies. AppLovin has said that it’s a priority to add advertisers to its “consumer” segment, which is primarily ecommerce.

    Criteo would offer a cheat code to get there.

    Recent findings suggest that the rise of residential proxy services that hide bot traffic behind real human IP addresses has been a boon for ad fraud. Often, consumers aren’t even aware they’re acting as a proxy for bot traffic.

    Now, cheap consumer electronics with backdoor vulnerabilities built in can deliver billions of fraudulent ad impressions per day, according to a new report by HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team.

    According to recent reports, the latest scheme Satori uncovered, which it dubbed BADBOX 3.0, was responsible for 40 billion fraudulent bid requests a day at its peak. It used the same residential proxy infrastructure as two other fraud rings that were uncovered by Satori in the past two years – hence the “3.0” branding.

    Recent findings suggest that the infrastructure relies on cheap TV sets manufactured in China by a company called TXCZ. These TVs have backdoors in their operating systems that allow fraudsters to compromise them.

    According to recent reports, once they’re compromised, the TVs run video ads in the background that the TV owner cannot see. The bid requests for these ads use the TV owner’s IP address to appear as if they’re targeted to a real human. They also impersonate traffic from legitimate CTV apps.

    People who bought one of these TVs pretty much had no chance.

    Industry observers note that “It was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers,” claims HUMAN’s Gavin Reid. “Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.”.

    YouTube adjusts its video view counts with modeled co-viewers based on its estimate of how many people saw the screen. [The Verge].

    Netflix is the frontrunner in a bidding war over the broadcast rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with experts expecting FIFA to charge up to $2 billion. [The Guardian].

    In a recent development, taylor Swift’s unveiled return to the Country Music Awards – her first appearance since 2013 – gave Disney and ABC a chance to squeeze more ad revenue from an event that had already sold out its inventory. [Variety].

    Industry observers note that the innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion.     #8418. Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (852 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Measuring Clicks Is Making ChatGPT Ads Look Like A Bad Bet

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The first question marketers ask about every latest advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?
    • Recent findings suggest that the debate around ChatGPT advertising has rapidly become a comparison with Google Search.
    • They’re all understandable questions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The first question marketers ask about every latest advertising channel is almost always the same: Does it perform better than the last one we tested?

    It happened with social. It happened with retail media. And now it’s happening with OpenAI.

    Recent findings suggest that the debate around ChatGPT advertising has rapidly become a comparison with Google Search. Can it deliver lower CPAs? Does it convert as well? Is it ready to compete for performance budgets?

    They’re all understandable questions. But they’re the wrong ones.

    It’s a mistake to assume conversational AI should behave like search in the first place. The customer journey is fundamentally different. If marketers continue evaluating ChatGPT using search-era metrics, there’s a real risk they’ll dismiss one of the most significant latest advertising channels before they’ve understood how it creates value.

    Google built the world’s most successful advertising business by harvesting intent.

    If a user searches for “cheap hotels in Hawaii,” Google shares a list of relevant results. The commercial intent is already there. The advertiser’s job is simply to be the most relevant answer when the purchase decision is made. But conversational AI works differently.

    Recent findings suggest that instead of typing in a few keywords, a user might go into detail and explain that they’re travelling to Hawaii for a friend’s wedding, that they’re on a tight budget but want their own room, oh, and they’d like to surf while they’re there. That’s no longer a search query; it’s a conversation. And that difference matters.

    Recent findings suggest that rather than simply capturing existing demand, conversational AI helps consumers explore options and refine priorities before they buy. When the traveler eventually visits the website to book, they’ve often already used AI to compare all the alternatives and understand exactly what they’re looking for.

    The advertising opportunity is participating in how intent develops.

    One of the first things marketers notice when they begin testing conversational AI is that the acquisition metrics can look uncomfortable.

    In a recent development, CPAs can appear higher than those achieved through search. For anyone used to judging performance through traditional attribution, that’s an easy reason to conclude the channel isn’t competitive.

    That was my first reaction, too.

    Recent findings suggest that if it looks like search and behaves like search, surely it should produce similar economics. But once you step back and look at the customer journey rather than the click, that conclusion becomes much harder to support.

    Industry observers note that A user spending several minutes discussing products, asking follow-up questions and refining their requirements is behaving very differently from someone typing a short keyword into Google. They’re effectively qualifying themselves before they ever reach an advertiser’s website.

    That means acquisition might cost more, but the customer arriving at the other end can also be significantly better informed and a much stronger commercial fit.

    Judging conversational AI purely on CPA risks confusing efficiency with effectiveness.

    The measurement frameworks we’ve inherited aren’t suited for where the consumer journey is going.

    Recent findings suggest that for more than two decades, performance marketing has been built around clicks because clicks were observable. Attribution models rewarded whichever interaction happened closest to the conversion, giving marketers a practical way to optimize campaigns at scale.

    That made perfect sense in an internet dominated by search engines, display advertising and relatively linear customer journeys.

    Conversational AI changes that, because the interaction influencing a purchase often happens long before a click ever occurs. And when the eventual conversion happens later through another channel, traditional attribution naturally gives the credit elsewhere.

    That doesn’t necessarily mean the initial conversation had little value; it simply means the measurement framework wasn’t designed to capture it.

    Early evidence suggests that when marketers move beyond attribution and begin measuring incremental business outcomes instead, conversational AI looks very different from the picture painted by last-click metrics.

    It has been revealed that AI advertising can work very effectively. But unless marketers are measuring it in a way that reflects how the channel actually influences buying decisions, it can create a colossal education gap.

    The conversation today largely centers on whether OpenAI can compete with Google.

    A far better question is whether conversational AI should be evaluated like search at all.

    Every evolution in advertising has forced marketers to rethink measurement. Social wasn’t simply another display channel. Retail media wasn’t just paid search inside a retailer’s website. CTV couldn’t be judged solely through linear TV metrics.

    Conversational AI deserves the same mindset shift.

    Sources indicate that google monetized search intent. Conversational AI has the potential to monetize the conversation that creates it.

    Recent findings suggest that those are fundamentally different commercial models. If marketers continue measuring one using the rules of the other, they risk underestimating not only the performance of OpenAI ads, but the role conversational AI is likely to play in the future of digital advertising.

    #8417. Meet OpenX’s New CEO, An Optimistic Realist

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1024 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Meet OpenX’s New CEO, An Optimistic Realist

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.
    • In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its new CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.
    • Horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Safari is cracking down on identity vendors, DSPs are going direct to publishers, Google gets to keep AdX, agents are threatening to cut out the middlemen, the walled gardens keep winning and the open web is under pressure.

    In early November, OpenX named Robert Horler as its new CEO, taking the reins from interim chief Joshua Metzger, who returned to his role as chief legal officer.

    Horler joins at a time of upheaval for the ad industry and one of readjustment for OpenX. In January, the company lost John “JG” Gentry, its CEO for nearly 15 years, after a long battle with cancer.

    A 30-year veteran of agencies, advertising and ad tech, Horler previously ran Dentsu Aegis Network in the US and Northern Europe, was COO of Quantcast and, most recently, led creator agency Whalar as chief exec before it was acquired by Accenture earlier this year. He’s still on the Whalar board.

    But, given the state of the industry, how was Horler feeling roughly a week in at OpenX? Not too bad. He’s a glass-half-full kinda guy, but he’s also a pragmatist.

    “Everybody’s being disrupted,” Horler stated. “You can pull the blanket over your head and say, ‘No thanks,’ or you can see an amazing amount of opportunity for companies that are agile and ambitious. I fancy our chances.”.

    Horler spoke with AdExchanger about Apple’s latest move, whether the sell side has the upper hand right now and the big boots he has to fill.

    According to recent reports, adExchanger: Let’s start with the state of play. The assumption for a long time was that as the line blurred between the buy side and sell side, DSPs would come out on top. Now it feels like the sell side has the power. Is that how you see it?

    ROBERT HORLER: I’d agree, but it’s complicated. The pendulum has swung toward supply because advertisers want to get closer to the data and the publisher.

    In a recent development, for the first time in about 30 years, the bigger agencies are pursuing divergent strategies for how they work with SSPs and DSPs. They all want more control, more orchestration and more influence over the revenue they drive, and I’d hypothesize that SSPs are well placed to deliver that.

    Also, no slight to The Trade Desk, but if the biggest cat in the jungle is having this many existential challenges, that tells you something’s going on.

    Industry observers note that speaking of big cats, OpenX is suing Google, as is Magnite, PubMatic and Index Exchange. I know there’s not much you can say about OpenX’s lawsuit, if anything, but as an industry observer, what did you think of the fact that Google didn’t have to divest AdX in the federal ad tech antitrust case?

    You know, it’s a shame. It’s tough for everybody who thought there would be one, but I can’t say that I’m surprised there wasn’t.

    According to recent reports, A lot of sell-side players are going buyer-direct. So is everything just everything now? Are the distinctions between buy-side and the sell-side tech no longer meaningful?

    For the people who aren’t in it, who don’t work in ad tech or programmatic advertising – and that includes some clients – the lines have always felt quite blurred. That’s not upcoming.

    In a recent development, there’s probably not as much difference now as there was, though. Things are converging and overlapping and people are encroaching a bit into each other’s territories as they figure out the brave fresh agentic landscape. And, of course, there are also pressures that exist within their own businesses.

    Industry observers note that but what will always be true is that publishers want to generate as much yield as possible and advertisers want to pay as little as possible, as long as it’s still effective, of course. So, yes, perhaps those lines are blurring a bit, but this natural tension will always exist.

    I know you’re still settling in, but how about you approaching Apple’s move to block identity vendors in iOS 27?

    Industry observers note that this is a major question that needs to be considered, and it’s not about workarounds; it’s about understanding it. I’m sure Joel [Meyer, OpenX’s CTO] and his team are all over it. But I don’t think it’s an existential challenge or that it represents a massively different challenge to other challenges we’ve had to navigate in the past in terms of privacy, control and all those good things.

    That’s all I can say right now other than that no one here is walking around and behaving like it’s an extinction event or something.

    Industry observers note that you spent the better part of a decade on the buy side, including as the US CEO of Dentsu. What do buyers get wrong about the sell side?

    I’d flip it, actually. The sell side needs to be simpler to partner with and more able to adapt, and sometimes they forget that. The sell side also underestimates how overwhelmed buyers are with choices.

    If you show up with an overly complex sell or a raft of products that you can’t explain in simple language, you’ll just sound like everyone else. Also, don’t underestimate the importance of humanity. Trust is built around people, not just technology.

    In a recent development, I wanted to ask about John. He was such a lovely man, and his death was such a loss. How will you keep his legacy alive?

    I never got to meet him, and I really wish I had. He was clearly beloved. When I came in for my board interview, I read the remembrance book here and it was really moving. It made me think, “If I get this job, those are major boots to fill.”.

    In a recent development, the best way to honor him is to continue the mission and build a valuable company where people enjoy coming into work. John clearly believed culture is preeminent and that it’s the people who make a great company, and I want to lead with that in mind.

    This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech firm DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook — and their respective short-form formats — as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.

    Sources indicate that doubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific. One thing those global respondents can agree on is their appreciation of YouTube. Google’s video hub is the most-used platform across all age groups and regions, with 95% of all respondents claiming to use it.

    Those users are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem. Half of the respondents remarked they would take action based on YouTube ads; that was the highest percentage among all measured platforms. Facebook came in second on that axis (49%), followed by Instagram (42%) and TikTok (38%).

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that other platforms are lagging behind in terms of actionable ads, and DoubleVerify’s findings suggest a big difference between those four industry leaders and their competitors. YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok are four platforms where short-form media has been widely adopted, and 38% of DoubleVerify respondents mentioned that short-form ads inspire them to take action. That was 7% higher than the next ad format on the list (long-form video pre-rolls, at 31%).

    It has been revealed that the ubiquity of short-form video is one factor that seems to be making ads more palatable across social media. Since the release of DoubleVerify’s 2025 Global Insights Report, 8% more consumers have decided that social media platforms are suitable locations for ads. YouTube, at 72%, was deemed the most valid platform for those spots.

    DoubleVerify’s report indicates that social media spend is paying off across multiple platforms, but marketers must still pick and choose as they allocate their ad dollars. As we saw with the Pew Research Center’s recent survey of American social media habits, usage data can vary wildly depending on demographic filters like age, gender, and household income.

    That assertion held true in the DoubleVerify report, in which TikTok ranked as the third most-used platform among 18-to-24-year-olds but didn’t crack the top five among the 65+ set. And most platforms skewed male worldwide, but 8% more female respondents use Pinterest compared to men.

    The global scope of DoubleVerify’s report adds another wrinkle to the conversation. In the Asia-Pacific region, for example, 56% of respondents noted that influencer activity “somewhat to significantly” impacted purchase decisions. In North America, that statistic is only 39%. So if marketers want to ensure that their social media activity inspires action, they should deploy their budgets wisely.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1037 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Don’t Give Privacy Regulators An Excuse To Come Knocking

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every time another state passes a privacy law or amends an existing one, brands have to tighten and upgrade their vendor contracts.
    • “If you’re doing business across state borders, your data goes everywhere,” said Patrick Turner, lead counsel for data and privacy at Ford Motor Company, speaking at an event hosted by the IAB in New York City this week focused on state privacy laws.
    • And so it makes sense for contracts to always meet the strictest combination of state requirements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every time another state passes a privacy law or amends an existing one, brands have to tighten and upgrade their vendor contracts.

    “If you’re doing business across state borders, your data goes everywhere,” said Patrick Turner, lead counsel for data and privacy at Ford Motor Company, speaking at an event hosted by the IAB in New York City this week focused on state privacy laws.

    And so it makes sense for contracts to always meet the strictest combination of state requirements.

    Sources indicate that but it’s a massive chore, and everyone – colleagues, partners, ad vendors – want to know why a contract that’s worked for years suddenly needs a rewrite, Turner remarked. They pummel him with questions.

    “Sometimes I’ll just turn off the microphone and scream into the wall briefly,” Turner joked, “because nobody hears you when you scream in space.”.

    The latest addition to Turner’s ever-growing to-do list comes courtesy of Delaware.

    In a recent development, in early September, Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer signed HB 380, an amendment to the state’s privacy law that takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and makes due diligence mandatory.

    Under the upcoming statute, companies can no longer assume a partner follows privacy laws just because it says so.

    It has been revealed that before sharing personal data with a third party, companies must now confirm the partner can actually meet its privacy obligations, using questionnaires and document reviews at a minimum. They also need a binding data-use contract in place. And it cuts both ways: Third parties of any size are required to cooperate with the due diligence process, and without a contract they aren’t allowed to process data at all.

    In programmatic advertising, though, vetting every partner in the supply chain would be a massive headache. A single ad campaign can bounce data between dozens of middlemen, measurement vendors and tracking pixels.

    And if every company in the chain sends every partner its own custom questionnaire, stated Michael Hahn, the IAB’s SVP and general counsel, “we drown ourselves in paperwork, and nobody is any safer.”.

    Sources indicate that but the sheer scale and complexity of ad tech doesn’t give companies a pass, remarked Delaware Deputy Attorney General John Eakins, who leads privacy enforcement for the state AG’s office. Sharing data through a massive programmatic network only heightens the risk to consumers, he added..

    “It requires a contract at each hop,” Eakins said, “because each hop is a transaction involving personal data.”.

    In other words, the days of box-ticking and boilerplate are finally over.

    Paperwork isn’t compliance, stated Courtney Cantor, deputy general counsel at PubMatic, who regularly fields a steady stream of due diligence requests.

    “It’s no longer about just putting the right contracts in place,” Cantor noted, “but actually having evidence to show if a regulator came knocking on your door.”.

    Although that’s assuming contracts reflect reality, which often isn’t the case.

    Take the standard clause requiring a vendor to delete everything when a customer agreement is terminated, said Gary Kibel, a partner at Davis+Gilbert. Not only do most companies not remember to do that; it’s often impossible.

    Sources indicate that “I can’t delete everything” is the correct response to any deletion request, Kibel noted, because vendors have legal and record-keeping obligations of their own. On top of that, if businesses purge all of their data, they can’t do business. If you delete a client’s email address, for example, then how do you chase an unpaid bill?

    The fact is, managing retention – which Turner referred to as “the ‘R’ word” – is borderline impossible, he said.

    “Everybody puts it in their agreements; everybody says how long they’ll keep things,” Turner said. “But I guarantee that if I went to every single person in this room’s company and looked at your data, I’d find retention violations everywhere.”.

    It’s not malicious or anything; it’s just incredibly difficult to do. “I don’t mean to inspire any attorneys general,” Turner noted, “but I think it’s an area we all have to be really careful about going forward.”.

    Although there’s a heck of a lot of low-hanging fruit to go after first. You’ve gotta get the basics sorted or you could be screwed.

    “I had a client about a year ago that got a letter from the Delaware attorney general’s office and they raised that issue,” he said.

    “The simple, easy things,” Turner said, “don’t let them be a problem.”.

    Sources indicate that and also don’t forget that regulators are also just people, he noted – people who read the news. When one company gets sued or fined, other states take notice and start wondering whether the same thing is happening in their backyard.

    Not that getting a letter from a regulator is necessarily a DEFCON 1 situation.

    These types of inquiries can feel scary because they often contain detailed questions, Kibel said. Regulators do their homework before reaching out. But a letter isn’t a formal legal demand, and companies don’t technically have to respond.

    It’s always a good idea to engage, though, Kibel said.

    Ignoring outreach from a regulator is a surefire way to turn a voluntary back-and-forth into a subpoena.

    Kibel has put clients on the phone with regulators in the past, and the vibe was usually as pleasant as could be expected. “It wasn’t treated like a deposition,” he mentioned, “and it wasn’t a hostile setting.”.

    Because regulators do “understand that every system is not 100% perfect,” Kibel noted.

    “But they also do want to see that you’ve thought about these issues in advance,” he stated, “and that you’re being forthright with them in terms of answering their questions.”.

    Ideally, the whole thing gets worked out over a few phone calls and never escalates.

    Likewise, the purpose of Delaware’s HB 380 isn’t for the AG’s office to chase down and investigate every single third party, Eakins said. The hope is that companies and their counsel do the policing themselves.

    “The goal is for the industry, for you all, to be saying, ‘You know what, this counterparty is just too much of a high risk,’” Eakins said. “I don’t trust what they’re doing with the data, so we’re just not going to take that reputational risk.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with.
    • That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.
    • Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy organization Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that different advertisers have different brand safety thresholds, but there are some topics that no one wants to be associated with. First and foremost: child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

    That risk is now playing out in Spain, where several advertisers paused their TikTok ads this week.

    Last week, Spanish news outlets reported that multiple advertisers – including Banco Santander and energy organization Moeve – had suspended their TikTok campaigns after ads from major Spanish brands had appeared alongside CSAM on the platform.

    Videos that either included CSAM or featured websites that sell CSAM ran before or after ads from 21 brands, Digiday reports, including Banco Santander, Samsung, Ralph Lauren and Pringles.

    TikTok has avoided taking direct responsibility in its recent statements, assuring advertisers and agencies in a note that it is “deeply committed” to ensuring that TikTok is a safe platform for teens and that it has a task force addressing the issue.

    “We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation,” a spokesperson tells Digiday (uh, duh), adding that it’s “categorically prohibited” on the platform.

    But, so far, these statements have done little to convince advertisers to return.

    It has been revealed that “Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia tells Digiday. So far, three of the agency’s clients have paused their TikTok activity.

    In a week of mass technology service outages across America, Chase wants you to know that its regular service has not been disrupted.

    However, one or more of Chase’s third-party tech vendors was the victim of a cyberattack. “We believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank wrote in a statement on Thursday.

    Mastercard and Visa were also tagged by a ransomware hacker org that leaked customer data. Credit card numbers were not compromised, but the data included some customer details. A Mastercard spokesperson described the leak as only touching a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” The Wall Street Journal reports.

    The disclosures leave many key questions unanswered. None of the companies has named the vendors involved or specified whose data was exposed and what it included. For example, did the leaked data belong to cardholders who consented to having their data used for marketing and analytics? That would be an interesting wrinkle.

    Chase was a little more specific about next steps, though, at least.

    “Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” it said in its response.

    On Thursday, Anthropic IPO’d at a cool $2 trillion, making it the first of the leading AI companies to go public.

    Its share price opened at $111.50, then dropped to roughly $100 within its first hour on the market.

    The timing is striking. Anthropic’s public launch comes just a week after ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his role at the manufacturer, following a leaked affair with a woman rumored to be a Chinese spy.

    In a recent development, huang’s departure left a gaping hole in AI funding. The industry may miss him for other reasons, too, but the bigger concern is capital.

    “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Shamillah Bankiya, a partner at Dawn Capital, tells TechCrunch. Colette Kress, Huang’s temporary replacement as Nvidia’s CEO, is expected to be “much more conservative,” another investor adds.

    Still, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO goes to show that the AI bubble isn’t at risk of popping quite yet.

    But it certainly “contrasts with an anxious moment for investors,” The Upcoming York Times writes, amid growing concerns over AI regulation and public backlash against the technology.

    According to recent reports, influencers claim creators can earn up to $5,000 by clipping Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay videos that hit a million views. In reality, YouTube Shorts typically pays just $30 to $100 per million views. [Benzinga].

    It has been revealed that also on the influencer front, Instagram creators are skeptical of the platform’s new affiliate program. [The Verge].

    Sources indicate that clinicians can now send prescriptions to patients via ChatGPT. [Adweek].

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that as Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That’s the gist of the Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.

    Industry observers note that the Fandom Fund follows up last year’s FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The upcoming collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

    Recent findings suggest that tubi won’t just pick any Kickstarter project; instead, as it has done with its other incubator programs, it will hone in on the genres that have the widest appeal among its 110 million monthly active customers. The categories fitting that description include horror, YA, Black entertainment, true crime, LGBTQ+, comedy, and reality.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Sources indicate that for Kickstarter, the Fandom Fund represents an increasing commitment to the creator economy. It is part of the three-month-old Culture Fund, which builds on Kickstarter’s enduring status as a key tool for indie artists. In 2024 alone, the platform generated over $700 million of fundraising across more than 35,000 projects.

    Recent findings suggest that indie creators don’t always get distribution deals with brand-name platforms, but Tubi is eager to support the next generation of storytellers — whom it believes are just as capable as traditional TV voices. To that end, Tubi has premiered a handful of demonstrates and movies led by social media standouts. One of the projects in the Fandom Fund will get a similar treatment by receiving additional backing, allowing it to be developed into a full-length series or feature film.

    “We believe great talent can come from anywhere,” said Tubi GM of Creator Programs and EVP of Business Development Rich Bloom in a statement. “The Fandom Fund gives emerging storytellers the resources to bring those ambitious ideas to life on a bigger canvas while preserving the creative voice, vision and ownership that made their work resonate.”.

    It has been revealed that kickstarter will provide updates about the Fandom Fund through its film-focused newsletter. Participation in the fund requires an active campaign, so if you want Tubi’s backing, get your crowdfunding game on.

    Q3 In Review: Pay TV Shrinks, Streaming And Sports Step Up

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?
    • Industry observers note that it’s a lot, we know.
    • Recent findings suggest that before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have you been keeping up with the quarterly earnings scoreboard for media and entertainment companies?

    Industry observers note that it’s a lot, we know. Not to worry. We figured you’d be busy, and so we tuned in to Q3 call after Q3 call so you didn’t have to. (You’re welcome.).

    Recent findings suggest that before you hunker down for Turkey Day, here’s a rundown on the TV and streaming companies (those that remain after all the recent consolidation, that is) that posted their earnings for the three months ending on Sept. 30 – and what these reports reveal about the state of TV and media today.

    Recent findings suggest that netflix’s Q3 numbers look decent on paper. Revenue rose 12% year over year to $12.9 billion, while advertising revenue alone has spiked over 80% this year. But Netflix wasn’t able to double its ad revenue again this year as planned. To be fair, growing ad revenue rapidly was easier to do back when Netflix first started its ads biz from scratch.

    On the advertising front, Netflix also touted improved programmatic targeting and ad measurement capabilities, including a pixel to measure conversions.

    It has been revealed that comcast’s media division reported $5.4 billion in earnings last quarter, a 13% YOY jump from this time last year. Alongside NBCUniversal, which Comcast intends to spin off as a standalone tech giant alongside British broadcaster Sky, Comcast’s media division also includes NBCU’s Peacock, Telemundo, Bravo and Universal film and television studios.

    According to recent reports, but Comcast had weaker performance across the broadband and theme park sides of the business, which saw a 6.1% revenue decline. (The theme parks live under the Universal brand and will go with NBCU and Sky in the spin-off.).

    Unlike Netflix, Fox boasted of recent boosts in engagement. Its free ad-supported TV platform, Tubi, saw a 23% YOY increase in viewing hours, thanks in part to the platform’s recent focus on creator content.

    Sources indicate that zooming out from Tubi, Fox’s overall revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion last quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue. But, sports and streaming aside, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. Fox News saw major viewership declines throughout the year and into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

    Sources indicate that fox was vague about details regarding its acquisition of Roku but asserted it expects to close the deal soon. A mere few days later, on Nov. 6, Fox announced it officially completed the acquisition.

    Versant Media, which spun off from Comcast in January, posted a 4% decline in Q3 revenue, a loss it mostly blamed on secular declines in the pay-TV industry.

    Versant also closed its acquisition of Full Swing last quarter, a deal that supports its ambitions to lean on live sports – golf in particular – as a competitive advantage.

    Skydance closed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 4, so there were no WBD-specific numbers in its Q3 report. But WBD aside, Skydance reported $7 billion in revenue last quarter, representing 5% YOY growth.

    Streaming was a highlight, with Paramount+ revenue jumping 21% YOY to just over $2.1 billion. Skydance also confirmed plans to launch a service combining HBO Max and Paramount+ at the beginning of next year.

    Skydance CEO David Ellison confirmed that Paramount+ and Pluto are officially operating on the same ad tech stack, noting that integrating HBO Max should be a relatively speedy process.

    Disney reported a 16% revenue jump to $25.9 billion in Q4 (its fiscal year ends in September) and a revenue increase of 8% to $102.3 billion for the full year.

    Recent findings suggest that ad revenue grew 10% to $1.7 billion within Disney’s entertainment segment. For its sports segment, that growth rate was 20%.

    Disney also shared that it’s unifying Disney+ and Hulu into one app beginning next month. The tech giant will add more sports to Disney+ in December and introduce creator content from TikTok into the Disney+ mobile app.

    Sports streamer Fubo, which also ends its fiscal year in September, saw its fourth-quarter revenue inch up to $1.5 billion from $1.48 billion during the same period last year.

    But Fubo suffered a net loss of $51.8 million in its Q4 – a heavier loss than the $38.8 million it posted in the same quarter last year. Fubo attributed the loss to operational and restructuring costs related to its recent merger with Hulu + Live TV.

    Thanks for reading and happy streaming!

    Turn target processes into epics engineers can build from directly: scenarios, acceptance criteria, increments.

    Design solutions within our reference architecture, and bring newly introduced patterns based on lessons learned.

    Lead technical delivery on your initiatives: plan increments with the engineers, manage dependencies and risks, and keep process owners and sponsors aligned on progress and decisions.

    Define and track value per initiative and increment, and keep business decisions moving.

    Feed delivery learnings back into the reference architecture, our delivery method and Camunda's product.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    7+ years in solution architecture or technical/process consulting, with an engineering background (Java, JavaScript or similar) and significant time delivering for the business or customers.

    A track record of leading process orchestration initiatives (Camunda or comparable) from discovery to production, not just designing them and handing over.

    Strong business analysis and process management skills: runs discovery and process redesign workshops with business stakeholders, models processes in BPMN, and turns the outcome into solid solution designs.

    Solution and data architecture in an enterprise context: integrations and APIs, and the data a process and its agents need across systems.

    An AI-first mindset, including first experience designing and building enterprise-grade agentic solutions.

    Sick of pirates and freebooters? Meta brings its “content protection” tool to Instagram.

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that pirated content has been an problem for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year.
    • Industry observers note that “Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook.
    • According to recent reports, once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that pirated content has been an problem for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.

    Industry observers note that “Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook’s video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube’s Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator’s video.

    According to recent reports, once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video. Notably, creators cannot receive monetization through the reposts, as is possible through services like Content ID.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Meta has positioned itself as a champion of original, non-repetitive content. It updated Instagram’s algorithm, providing more visibility for creators who share their own work. Financial penalties for serial reuploaders came to Facebook in 2025, and further penalties arrived on Instagram this year.

    Other platforms have followed Meta’s lead. YouTube cracked down on “mass-produced or repetitive” content in 2025. Earlier this year, Google’s video hub clarified that creators aren’t able to monetize “generic” uploads. Anything “unsatisfying or off-putting” — i.e. the sort of slop you’d expected a generative AI model to spit out — faced similar repercussions.

    Industry observers note that the link between unoriginal reuploads and AI slop is undeniable. Traditional studios have urged platforms to crack down on channels that use AI to steal from artists rather than executing original concepts. Those demands have led to new rules across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

    Industry observers note that by bringing content protection to Instagram, Meta is setting itself up to take further action against AI slop in the future. An introductory post explains that “we’re also exploring different ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly,” so stay tuned for that if you’re sick of low-effort AI posts.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers: Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search, all deeply integrated.

    Sources indicate that developers decide what to build with by listening to people they trust, much of it on Twitter, where Supabase's community, launches, and competitors are all discussed in public. We want a senior DevRel leader who is already a known, trusted voice there, to be a brand ambassador for Supabase. You'll work alongside our Latest Media and DevRel teams and help shape how Supabase indicates up in these conversations. We hire for the voice and following you already have.

    Be a visible, trusted voice for Supabase on Twitter: post, reply, and join developer conversations daily.

    Share sharp, useful content, from introduces and tips to opinions on where building is going.

    Represent Supabase at events, on podcasts, and in the wider developer community.

    Bring developer feedback to engineering and product, and work with Upcoming Media, DevRel, and PMM on rolls out.

    You have an existing, engaged Twitter following. We'll look at who you talk to and how people respond, as well as follower count.

    You have senior experience in DevRel, developer advocacy, or a similar developer-facing role.

    You're credible with a technical audience and a strong writer with a distinctive voice.

    You're comfortable representing a company publicly, on camera, on stage, and online.

    Recent findings suggest that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    In a recent development, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    According to recent reports, supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #8380. As Netflix and Disney sniff around, YouTube hypes its creators’ “world-class, studio-quality” programming at L.A. Premieres event

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2466 w)
