    AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital.
    • Industry observers note that your AI visibility dashboard highlights brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources.
    • Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

    Industry observers note that your AI visibility dashboard highlights brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

    Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

    AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

    What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

    As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

    However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

    These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

    The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

    Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

    TransPerfect Digital explains how its team ranks AI search opportunities by business impact and the effort each change would take.

    The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

    A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

    Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

    Industry observers note that imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

    If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

    To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

    Recent findings suggest that that means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

    Pro Tip: Before relying on a visibility score, check whose questions it represents. See how we choose prompts for each audience and buying stage.

    To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:.

    Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

    Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

    Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

    According to recent reports, list the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

    Prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:.

    It has been revealed that the second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

    Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

    That description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different matter.

    It has been revealed that before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:.

    Match your response to what the answer actually says:.

    Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

    Industry observers note that the third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

    It has been revealed that suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your plan, examine the cited discussions.

    A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

    Prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:.

    See how we prioritize changes to content, technical SEO, and third-party sources when several findings compete for the same team’s time.

    The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

    Sources indicate that A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

    Recent findings suggest that low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

    Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:.

    Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

    Before assigning work, review these four questions:.

    Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

    For a closer look at measurement, see how we separate measurable AI referrals from signs of AI influence.

    #8303. A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1031 w)

    A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov.
    • Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a company that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.
    • Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

    Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a company that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

    Optimizely’s status page notes an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the firm remarked the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

    Sources indicate that the way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

    Report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

    Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer says the organization has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”.

    Helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

    Industry observers note that helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

    Recent findings suggest that the Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

    In a recent development, seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

    It has been revealed that helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

    Industry observers note that optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

    Sources indicate that helme says the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your users, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

    It has been revealed that the change history page from Optimizely claims that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

    Optimizely’s documentation example below demonstrates the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

    Industry observers note that project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

    Recent findings suggest that optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

We're building the best developer platform to power the next generation of software companies, and our go-to-market team is scaling fast to match.

    According to recent reports, we're looking for a lead in Go-To-Market Strategic Planning, to shape how Supabase's GTM engine runs. This is a high-leverage, high-ownership role that sits at the intersection of strategy, data, and execution. You'll work directly with Success, Sales, Marketing, Finance, Partnerships and Product to build the systems, processes, and insights that help our go-to-market teams move faster and smarter.

    Own the end-to-end GTM Strategic Planning, covering territory design, segmentation design, target planning and GTM capacity planning.

    Build and maintain a single source of truth for planning data across HubSpot, BigQuery and Hex.

    Translate organization priorities into field actions through designing the planning strategy and seeing it through to execution.

    Define and track the metrics that matter, and surface insights that drive action, not just reporting.

    Lead the Strategic Planning roadmap: guide and lead in tooling investments and evaluate newly introduced systems and processes against real business needs.

    Work cross-functionally with talent acquisition, ensuring GTM and territory models stay aligned.

    Collaborate with GTM Engineering on automations and data pipelines so that your strategy translates into working systems, not just slide decks.

    According to recent reports, bridge strategy and execution. From drafting segmentation approaches in Google Docs to using SQL to monitor its effectiveness.

    Recent findings suggest that build for scale without over-engineering. Simple systems that work beat perfect systems that don't ship.

    Recent findings suggest that stay close to the customer. Developers are our buyers, and understanding how they discover, adopt, and expand is core to everything you'll do.

    #8295. Latest Update: Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2020 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the routine is familiar by now.
    • In a recent development, I’ve watched this for most of 20 years.
    • When Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

    In a recent development, I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

    When Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post said what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how massive it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

    Here is the entry for the November 2026 core update, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

    Industry observers note that google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it said it changes Search thousands of times a year and announces the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t revealed at all. So a named revision is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

    The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

    The date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

    It has been revealed that what neither of them indicates is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

    Sources indicate that that hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November upgrade within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

    The closest thing I know to a core upgrade is the annual performance review.

    Anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

    According to recent reports, A core enhancement is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

    The comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core upgrade you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

    The strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

    There’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content upgrade to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who claims most affected sites had it coming.

    Look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the glitch, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

    Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

    Recent findings suggest that most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and released.

    According to recent reports, when that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an update window and gets blamed on the update.

    Then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

    This is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

    Sources indicate that so there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the upgrade coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

    This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

    Recent findings suggest that take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation states it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

    Industry observers note that the traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

    Recent findings suggest that “JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

    If quality is a list of items to tick, then a core update is a latest edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

    So people who hold quality as a checklist need each update explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

    The first question a business could ask after an update is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

    Now read the PDF from the patch before. It claims the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

    The second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site launched.

    The fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

    Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

    Industry observers note that the line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no upgrade, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

    In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

    It has been revealed that google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.

    This post was originally published on The Inference.

    #8286. Tech Report: Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan.
    • Industry observers note that I found this out the practical way.
    • Industry observers note that I scanned them and moved on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan. 1, 2027. You may have deleted it because you don’t advertise in Europe. Don’t assume you’re off the hook. Google bills these surcharges based on where your ads are actually served, and its default location setting can serve your ads to people who have never set foot in your target area.

    Industry observers note that I found this out the practical way. I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account. His campaigns are built to reach shoppers within a few miles of his store. On the morning of Nov. 11, his account received two notices from Google Payments, one headed “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in Italy” and the other “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in France.”.

    Industry observers note that I scanned them and moved on. Then I went back, because I suspected plenty of Search Engine Journal readers were asking the same question I was. Why is a neighborhood retailer in New York getting billing notices about two countries he isn’t targeting?

    Industry observers note that the short answer is that the emails are a warning, not a bill. Whether they become a bill depends on settings most local advertisers have never opened.

    Sources indicate that google calls these charges jurisdiction-specific surcharges. Some are labeled Digital Services Tax (DST) fees and some are labeled Regulatory Operating Costs, but they work the same way. They are added to your invoice on top of your ad spend, and on top of any account budget you set.

    Recent findings suggest that here is how the rates for Google Ads stand on Google’s help page, before and after Jan. 1, 2027.

    Two former entries are off the list. Google claims ads served in India stopped carrying a 2% charge on Sept. 1, 2024, and ads served in Canada no longer carry the 2.5% DST fee.

    The same increases apply to Display & Video 360, and Google’s help page says YouTube placements bought on a reservation basis carry the surcharges too.

    In Italy, the jump is half a point. In France, it is a full point, which means the fee itself rises by 50%. Turkey moves the other way.

    See also: Ask A PPC: How Will The Tariffs Impact My PPC Campaigns?

    Google’s help page states the rule plainly. The charge applies every time an ad is served in one of these jurisdictions, “regardless of where your actual business is located.” The surcharge is calculated on the impressions or clicks served in each country, so an account that serves nothing in France pays nothing in France.

    That would seem to settle it for my client. But a few paragraphs further down, Google adds a warning that you might show ads to users in a country you never targeted “because your business is in a location of interest for them.” Google also says it is the advertiser’s responsibility to make sure campaign target settings are correct, and that it will not refund surcharges triggered by legitimate clicks and impressions served according to those settings.

    In plain English, if your settings let a shopper in Milan see your ad, you pay the Italy surcharge on that impression, and you don’t get it back.

    See also: 13 Google Ads Settings To Check When Running International PPC Campaigns.

    It has been revealed that google’s advanced location options give you two choices for who counts as being in your target area. “Presence or interest” reaches people who are in, regularly in, or who’ve shown interest in your targeted locations. “Presence” reaches only people who are in or regularly in them.

    Presence or interest is the default, and Google labels it as recommended. Google supports that recommendation with its own data, saying advertisers in travel, real estate, and education who switched to it saw 5% more conversions on Search campaigns. That is Google’s claim from Google’s internal data, and it covers three verticals, not retail.

    It has been revealed that for a store on Madison Avenue, “interest” is where Europe gets in. Someone in Paris searching for shops on the Upper East Side has shown interest in New York. Under the default, your ad can serve to that person, and the impression lands in France.

    It has been revealed that the controls have also been widening. Demand Gen campaigns picked up the same Presence or interest versus Presence choice in late 2025, and AI Max for Search has added options for reaching people based on locations of interest. More automation in where ads go means more chances to serve impressions in places you didn’t pick.

    It has been revealed that giovanni Perilli, a funnel marketing consultant who writes about European ad costs, published a breakdown the same day the emails went out. The France email he received did not mention Italy at all. In his words, the email “leaves out the change that matters most to anyone advertising in Italy.”.

    That matches my own experience, with a twist. My client’s account got two separate emails, one per country. Advertisers who received only one should check the help page rather than assume nothing else changed.

    Industry observers note that perilli also turns the surcharge into numbers a PPC manager can use. Because the fee is added on top of what you spend, he multiplies a cost-per-acquisition by 1.03 and divides a return on ad spend by 1.03. A €40 CPA effectively becomes €41.20. A ROAS of four becomes about 3.88. If your break-even ROAS is 2.5, your real target in France and Italy is now about 2.58.

    It has been revealed that those are small numbers. On thin retail margins in the first quarter, they are not nothing.

    See also: Google Indicates Changing tCPA & Budgets Won’t Reset Learning – 6 BFCM Takeaways.

    Google’s help page indicates the France and Italy charges cover part of the cost of complying with digital services tax legislation in those countries. The tax news over the past year lines up with that.

    French lawmakers voted in October 2025 to double France’s digital services tax from 3% to 6% for the largest platforms, but the budget bill carrying it was rejected a month later, and the rate remains 3%. Italy’s DST has applied at a 3% rate since 2020, and its 2025 budget law removed the domestic revenue threshold that had kept some companies out of scope. Turkey went the other direction, cutting its DST from 7.5% to 5% this year and to 2.5% on Jan. 1, 2027. Google’s Turkey surcharge falls to 2.25% on the same date.

    Google also has company now. Meta began charging its own location fees on July 1, 2026, at 3% in France, Italy, and Spain, as Bloomberg reported. From January, Google and Meta charge the same 3% in all three countries.

    Here’s my read. Digital services taxes were sold to voters as a way to make significant tech pay. The platforms are now itemizing those taxes on advertisers’ invoices, and some of those advertisers are small businesses on another continent. Whatever you think of the policy, the bill has moved down the chain, and PPC managers are the ones who have to explain it to clients.

    Here are four steps I’m taking in my client’s account, and I’d suggest you take them in yours.

    I almost ignored these notices, and I’ve been reading Google Ads billing emails since 2003. My advice is to treat them as an audit prompt, not as spam. The surcharge itself is modest. The real story is how many local accounts may be serving ads in Europe without anyone deciding they should.

    Recent findings suggest that my client’s ads are meant for the Upper East Side, not Paris or Milan. I’d rather confirm that in a report before Jan. 1 than discover it on a February invoice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    In a recent development, we are looking for a Senior Contracts Manager to take ownership of vendor contracting at Supabase. You will be the go-to contracts partner for everything we buy.

    This is a hands-on, high-autonomy role with real ownership, for an experienced negotiator who takes pride in making procurement faster while managing risk. You will negotiate directly, build the playbooks and workflows that let the business self-serve on low-risk deals, and escalate the right issues to Legal at the right time. We work AI-first in Legal: you will use Claude and Ironclad every day to move faster and with greater accuracy. Your work will shape how procurement and vendor contracting scale as Supabase grows.

    Own vendor contracting end to end.

    Review, draft, and negotiate a high volume of vendor agreements, including MSAs, order forms, SOWs, SaaS and cloud subscription terms, DPAs, and NDAs.

    Serve as the single point of contact for all vendor contracting matters raised by FinOps, IT, Security, and business owners, from intake through signature, renewals, amendments, disputes, and offboarding. As capacity allows, you will also support the broader Commercial Legal team on other matters.

    Apply and further build out our playbook and risk framework independently, and escalate to the Assistant General Counsel, Commercial where a deal falls outside approved positions or raises novel legal risk.

    Negotiate data, privacy, and security terms (DPAs, security exhibits, cross-border transfers) within the Security team’s playbook, and bring in the AGC, Commercial or Privacy for anything outside it.

    Review AI vendor terms, such as training on our data, output ownership, and model changes.

    Build and scale vendor contracting operations.

    Build out and maintain our vendor playbook in Claude, so the whole team works from the same guidance and low-risk deals move without bottlenecks.

    Design and improve intake, triage, and approval workflows with FinOps.

    In a recent development, own the vendor and procurement workflow in Ironclad, including intake, templates, approvals, and the repository, working with Legal Ops, who own the platform. Use it to track renewals and notice windows with FinOps and flag spend concentration risks.

    Create training and self-serve resources for business partners, and raise the visibility of the contracts function as a business enabler.

    Recent findings suggest that 6 to 8+ years of experience negotiating procurement, vendor, or technology transactions contracting, ideally buy-side at a U.S. SaaS or technology organization, with deep knowledge of SaaS, cloud, and software licensing terms.

    A track record of negotiating directly with vendors and their counsel, independently and at pace.

    Strong working knowledge of privacy, data protection, and security terms in commercial contracts, including DPA negotiation and international data transfers.

    Experience designing contracting processes that are consistent, transparent, and easy for the business to follow.

    Clear writing and speaking, with the ability to explain legal and commercial risk plainly and the judgment to know when to hold a position, approve a reasonable risk, or escalate.

    Comfort using AI tools, Claude in particular, with sound judgment about when to rely on outputs, how to verify them, and how to protect confidential information.

    A degree in a relevant field (for example, law, economics, or political science), though we value experience over the specific degree.

    Sell-side experience negotiating customer, partner, or reseller agreements for a SaaS or technology company, which helps you see vendor terms from the other side.

    Hands-on experience with Ironclad or a similar CLM tool (Juro, Docusign CLM) or building AI-assisted legal workflows, ideally with some exposure to AI governance.

    Experience working across jurisdictions or with distributed, international teams.

    Experience at a fast-growing, developer-focused, cloud, security, or open source organization.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Industry observers note that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Industry observers note that once a year, the entire organization gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Sources indicate that data was provided by Verso, which tracks users’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account. The sample size is 41,961 conversations, generated by 12,321 people between Jan. 1 and Oct. 29, 2026. Most of the figures are from a sub-sample which had been statistically weighted to match the demographic characteristics of the U.S. population.

    Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business. Based on the analysis, Rand Fishkin (co-founder and CEO of SparkToro) concluded that the primary reason AI visibility matters is Google’s implementation of AI Overviews and AI Mode, rather than ChatGPT itself.

    Sources indicate that based upon the purchase-intent graph developed with the weighted group, there are three types of conversation by purpose. In a total of 4.9% of conversations, the person planned to purchase and was continuing to look at the options; another 2.1% were asking questions related to purchasing a specific brand, product or service; while a total of 93.1% showed no intention to purchase.

    Fishkin wrote, “I suspect this is bad news for ChatGPT’s advertising opportunities.”.

    It has been revealed that he also referenced SparkToro’s December 2024 analysis of approximately 332 million Google searches. He wrote that 15% or more of searches fit his definition. SparkToro did an analysis of searches done by a U.S. panel via browsers from January 2023 through September 2024. Commercial (a financial, business services or commerce intent) accounted for 14.5% of searches, although the searcher may not have been ready to make a purchase at that time.

    Transactional accounted for 0.69%. These categories do not match the categories identified in the ChatGPT graph which measured purchase intentions, so the percentages cannot be compared directly.

    It has been revealed that in addition to tracking whether people asked about brands, the report also tracked if ChatGPT’s responses named any. In the weighted group, 86.7% of all prompts did not ask for brand, product or organization information. Of all prompts, 6.6% asked about several brands, with the remainder being about a single brand (6.7%). On the response side, 7.0% of all responses mentioned multiple brands, products or companies while 5.1% mentioned one; the post’s reported percentage of responses mentioning at least one was 12.1%.

    The post’s takeaways describe 12% of ChatGPT usage as part of the buyer journey, though its purchase-intent chart puts conversations with purchase intent at 6.9%.

    Sources indicate that images and visual design requests were the top ranked category in the report with a total of 17.6% of conversations. Information and entertainment came second in terms of overall conversations (14.4%), writing and communication third (12.7%), while shopping, brands and local services made up 5.3%.

    One category per conversation was assigned, representing the primary goal of each. The output type counts over the topic when someone asks ChatGPT to create something (e.g., if you ask it to write an email asking for a refund from PayPal, that would be categorized as writing instead of shopping).

    Recent findings suggest that the percentages shown in the report’s chart vary from the percentages shown in the report’s text by less than two percentage points per category. The percentages provided here reflect the report’s chart.

    The panel was also compared to OpenAI’s Signals data for September using the weighted group. OpenAI’s data was heavier towards writing and tech support, while the weighted panel data leaned more toward image requests and how-to questions. The author says the two are fair to compare given that OpenAI almost certainly includes API requests (that Verso does not track) in its numbers.

    Sources indicate that according to OpenAI’s page, the dataset “reflects only messages within ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, and Pro accounts” and Codex and enterprise usage are excluded from this count; thus excluding API calls as well. In addition, OpenAI presents global message shares whereas the panel shows shares of U.S.-based conversations.

    Verso offers a free tool that breaks down a person’s ChatGPT history. Its sign-up terms say Verso stores the imported conversations and includes them, de-identified, in datasets it licenses to research and business customers. According to the post, Verso co-founder Aaron Aknin reached out to the post’s author and supplied the data.

    Sources indicate that the report also described the panel as skewed toward younger people, women and people at lower income levels. There were 9,675 members in the panel that had demographic information that could be used as a weighting base to match the 2024 United States Census. No usage category varied by more than 1.4 percentage points when the demographics were weighted to these standards.

    Before the data analysis was performed, the 131 heaviest customers, who generated an average of over 33 prompts per active month, were eliminated. These heavy users accounted for approximately 1% of the total number of panelists, but they were responsible for sending 21% of all prompts. On average each member of the weighted group (excluding the above noted heaviest users) sent 9.9 prompts between January and October.

    Sources indicate that as most panelists were recorded on mobile phones, the post says this may have caused some of the usage through desktop computers and work accounts to be underreported. API requests are not included in the data set.

    Each conversation was coded using a written code book provided to Anthropic’s model called Claude. Each conversation was coded based upon its title, up to six of the user-generated prompts, the initial few lines of ChatGPT’s first few responses and any product cards or bolded names. A second coder independently recoded a random sample of conversations, and the two coders agreed on categories 90% of the time and on brand tags 97% to 99% of the time. The post reports no separate agreement figure regarding its identification of purchase intent.

    SparkToro sells audience research software.

    In a recent development, for brands splitting AI visibility and ad budgets, the U.S. panel gives a measured share of ChatGPT conversations that involve buying, and it’s under 7%. Fishkin concludes that Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode are what make AI visibility key, and he questions whether tracking ChatGPT visibility is worth it unless Bing rankings and AI visibility are tracked too.

    It has been revealed that the post explains that the panel reflects what people ask ChatGPT much better than how often they use it. For PPC teams exploring ChatGPT Ads, the 6.9% purchase-intent share offers a snapshot of the conversation mix in a consumer panel with light ChatGPT use, not a count of purchase-related conversations across ChatGPT.

    Industry observers note that until panel data includes desktop, work and API use, it’s best to pair purchase-intent figures like this one with your own ChatGPT referral and ad data before adding them to a budget proposal. Fishkin also shared that he looks forward to doing more research with Verso.

    #8272. Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance.
    • Recent findings suggest that illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests.
    • CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance. They also share that attempts to control crawler traffic can sometimes accidentally block Googlebot and harm Search visibility.

    Recent findings suggest that illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests. Google’s automated crawling systems interpret the improved performance as an indication that more crawling is possible and responds by gradually increasing the crawl rate.

    CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.

    When Google increases the crawl rate, the initial crawl is handled by the origin server. But now Googlebot is hitting the server more aggressively and it’s this that can overwhelm the origin server, initially.

    “For one, suddenly the crawling metrics suggests the site can handle a larger amount of crawling. And on the flip side, because the CDN caches aren’t yet populated, the origin server still has to serve the requested pages.

    Basically, CDNs take the valve off the hose, so now crawlers are drinking from a fire hose.”.

    Cherry Prommawin added more details:.

    “Under normal circumstances, our crawlers operate under an important rule. When a server responds faster, the crawlers assume the infrastructure is healthy and slowly ramp up crawl speed.

    …So the crawlers see how fast the server responds, get really excited, and start to crawl the entire site at a higher, higher, and higher speed. But it’s a trap.

    People assume a CDN can catch a crawl spike from day one, but …The cache has to be filled up with the assets off the site first.”.

    Gary Illyes explained that on a first request for a page the CDN has to fetch the page from the origin server first to populate the cache with the content. It’s not until the second request for the page that the cache is populated with the content and begins doing its job.

    “…which means your origin server may get slammed by the flood anyway. Now, to be fair, our crawlers take time to ramp up. It won’t happen in a millisecond.

    According to recent reports, an empty cache means your origin server is still doing all the heavy lifting. Until that cache is populated, your CDN isn’t acting as a shield just yet.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A CDN cannot serve an un-cached URL without retrieving it first from the origin server and that only happens after a request for that URL is first made. Crawlers visit large numbers of URLs virtually all the time and can generate a substantial amount of origin traffic before the CDN’s caches are fully populated.

    Recent findings suggest that this next issue involves accidentally blocking Googlebot and triggering a reduced search presence because Google can no longer crawl and index URLs from a website. Illyes and Prommawin explain it in the context of a website admin flipping a switch at Cloudflare and inadvertently blocking Googlebot.

    This is a real problem, I recall an instance in which a popular website’s massive traffic dried up whenever Cloudflare was activated and would return once they turned it off. They had a devil of a time diagnosing why this was happening and the customer service people at the time were unable to help them. It may have been the case, as Illyes and Prommawin noted, that the admin had turned on a strict bot filter that inadvertently blocked Googlebot.

    Illyes offered an example of an admin doing exactly that:.

    “They look at the spiking traffic, assume they are being aggressively scraped by botnets, and naturally, they panic.”.

    And what sometimes happens next is that an admin might turn on “blanket security rules” that block Googlebot.

    Prommawin offered more details:.

    …If the CDN detects automated requests, it intercepts them with a CAPTCHA challenge, asking them to click pictures of traffic lights to prove they’re human.

    …It sees automated requests, flags it as a bot, and then intercepts with a CAPTCHA. And since our crawlers cannot identify a traffic light, they fail the test.”.

    What eventually happens with prolonged Googlebot blocking is that Google will begin dropping the pages from the index.

    Sources indicate that prommawin suggested that site admins should configure their CDN to allow known and trusted crawlers. This is a method called whitelisting where only crawlers that are on the “allowed” list can get it and all other crawlers cannot.

    They also recommend the use of CDN-level rate limiting of Googlebot if the requests on the origin server lead to downtime which can negatively impact legitimate human traffic to the website.

    When a site initially starts out with a CDN, the CDN does not have a cache of a website’s content. The cache doesn’t get loaded until it’s requested by a browser or crawler visit.

    Industry observers note that cache pre-warming is the process of requesting content from a site so that the content gets loaded onto the CDN. This ensures that the content is already loaded onto the CDN before consumers request it, which ensures that the content is delivered quickly without the CDN having to first retrieve it from the origin server (the server where the actual content files exist).

    Illyes recommends “pre-warming” the cache by programmatically requesting URLs from it so that thE cache is populated in a controlled manner.

    “And to survive augmenting your site with a CDN, see if you can pre-warm the caches by programmatically fetching your top URLs through the CDN before you open the floodgates to search engines.”.

    Sources indicate that google’s main point is that moving to a CDN can create an unexpected combination of faster crawling and increased origin-server demand. That in turn can lead to unintentionally setting aggressive security restrictions that prevent Googlebot from accessing a website.

    Three especially important points for SEOs and site owners:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. Using a CDN can trigger an increase in Googlebot crawling when it detects faster server responses, even though the CDN’s caches have not yet been populated, which in turn means an increase in requests for URLs from the origin server.

    It has been revealed that 2. A CDN migration can inadvertently cause pages to disappear from Google Search due to aggressive security settings intended to stop malicious bots can also lock out Google’s crawlers.

    Sources indicate that 3. Google recommends pre-warming caches, allowing trusted crawlers, and temporarily controlling crawling when server demand becomes excessive.

    Read Google’s new CDN documentation here.

    The screen-time debate’s blind spot

    📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (71 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Eschoolnews

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read

    It has been revealed that last fall, during a professional development session I was running with a group of teachers in São Paulo, a fifth-grade teacher raised her hand and asked a question I have since heard in every country I work in: “I want to use AI to plan better lessons.     Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

    New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

    Sources indicate that proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

    In a recent development, some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

    According to recent reports, participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

    Sources indicate that this effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

    There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

    “I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman mentioned. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a Upcoming York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

    Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

    RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson stated in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”.

    Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

    Recent findings suggest that upcoming York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

    “It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin mentioned.

    RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

    To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

    Recent findings suggest that the team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

    There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

    One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, noted Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

    Sources indicate that “When reading a text, for example, people can swiftly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”.

    Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

    In a recent development, the group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

    San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” noted that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”.

    Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard remarked.

    Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

    She mentioned labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”.

    #8264. Google Ads AI Max Is Making More Decisions For You – 6 Settings To Audit Now via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)
